source: Adam selected #111 and asked to finish its implementation, then stop for review, in chat on 29 October 2026. Issue: https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/111.
next: Review the #111 project progress, real run timeline and labelled synthetic comparisons; discuss the five learning questions. No later stage, human acceptance or issue closure is inferred.
decisions: This is a developer tool, separate from the shipped map app. Pi tool wiring is being checked with prepared responses before live AI calls.
Define (#103) is closed. Adam selected Connect (#104) as the next stage on 22 October 2026. This records the decision to advance, not unrecorded answers to the learning questions.
Rootless Podman now runs the trusted calibration checks in disposable containers. Pi will stay outside; Bubblewrap is not needed initially.
The container boundary passed trusted live demonstrations. Adam then asked to commit and continue; this is recorded separately from approval of later Pi/model checkpoints.
Results and reports stay on this machine, outside Git history.
Pi chooses investigation and repair steps within permitted tools. Our runner enforces scope, execution, budgets, required checks and stopping conditions.
Connect adds startup checks and structured tool outcomes. Recover (#106) adds a compact session handoff reconciled against files, journal and receipts.
The first Connect slice inspects local Podman runtime prerequisites and records a separate readiness receipt. It does not execute candidates or demonstrate container isolation.
After the readiness walkthrough, Adam asked to commit and proceed on 22 October 2026. This approves the readiness slice; later container and Pi checkpoints still need their own evidence and review.

The first live checkpoint used Podman v6.1.4 and a fixed prepared image ID. Good passed, wrong failed as intended, dummy host access was denied and timeout/cancellation containers were confirmed removed. Kernel resource settings were read, not stress-tested.

The app session lacked the CPU controller while the user manager already delegated it. A transient systemd user service reports CPU, memory and pids; no sudo or global configuration change was needed.
Adam asked to commit and continue after reviewing the container/report work. It is committed locally as f61485f; nothing has been pushed.
Adam wants provider and model selectable locally, using whichever supported subscription he has. He currently has a Codex subscription. API-key billing is not authorised as a fallback.
Pi v1.2.0 is pinned in a separate developer package, with install scripts disabled and this machine's existing seven-day npm cooldown preserved.

The first Pi slice uses prepared responses through the actual SDK and four controlled Python tools. Project checks still run in restricted rootless Podman containers. This does not test AI reasoning or establish subscription access.

Adam selected local defaults: provider openai, model gpt-6.1-sol, subscription auth, ten model requests and 4096 output tokens per request. Pi needs its own supported sign-in; Codex tokens are not copied. Live model execution stays disabled for this checkpoint.

Adam clarified that both subscription provider and exact model must be configurable for Codex or Claude. The current local Codex choice is not a hard-coded provider/model. Existing setup was verified with two catalogue models for each of openai and anthropic, using isolated temporary configuration and no model calls. Live execution remains a later checkpoint.

The first login attempt failed before browser authorisation because the wrapper omitted the installation ID callback. Reproduced with the real SDK, then fixed by persisting/reusing Pi's existing settings identity and passing the harness app name. Known error messages are now actionable without printing token responses. A temporary-settings check reached the browser authorisation prompt and cancelled cleanly; real account sign-in remains for Adam.

Adam confirmed sign-in. The local setup status reports signedIn true, provider openai, model gpt-6.1-sol and subscription auth. Zero model calls have been made; live model execution remains disabled. No live model access or checkpoint acceptance is inferred from this sign-in status.

Adam asked to commit the prepared Pi tool wiring, subscription setup and reporting changes, then explain where each part lives. This authorises the commit; it does not close #104 or mark a live model run complete.

Adam asked to run the agent. Added a subscription model path, request/payload guards and model identity/usage evidence. A circular CLI import stalled the first launch before model work; cancellation removed its Pi process and three startup containers. A separate CLI entry point and real-process startup check fix that wiring error.

The next launch reached the real OpenAI subscription adapter. It omitted the output-token cap, so our payload guard blocked before inference and before any edit. A no-network reproduction with the actual adapter and dummy OAuth credential confirms zero fetch calls. OpenAI preview-limitations documentation explicitly lists max_output_tokens as unsupported. No API billing fallback or relaxed limit was used.

Adam asked to switch the local model from gpt-6.1-sol to gpt-6-luna. Subscription auth and existing request/output limits are retained. This changes model selection only; it does not authorise removing the hard output-token cap. Historical Sol receipts retain their original model identity.

Adam authorised running without a hard output-token cap, retaining timeouts and analysing actual usage. Local gpt-6-luna subscription settings now use maxOutputTokensPerRequest null, ten model requests, low reasoning, one edit/check, 12 tools and a ten-minute deadline. Each provider request also has a two-minute HTTP timeout. API-key fallback and automatic retries remain disabled.

The first real Luna run completed in 96.0761 seconds with five model requests and six tool calls. It read the three permitted files, searched import.go, edited once and requested the fixed sandboxed test. Its candidate failed all GPX/TCX/KML cases; Luna acknowledged the failure. All four containers were removed. Outcome repair_failed is a model repair failure, not an execution/setup blocker or stage approval.

Complete provider usage for that run: 51,284 input tokens, 329 output tokens, 51,613 total; zero cached-input and zero reasoning tokens reported. Largest response 172 output tokens; no response exceeded the earlier 4096-token cap. Input and output are totals across five requests, including repeated conversation history. One run does not establish typical usage or a future output bound. Local evidence: reports/harness/pi/runs/743759ebfff84ae48c2c6ac3236aa7e4/.

After the plain-language explanation of the first failed attempt, Adam asked to try again with bounded timings. Kept Luna, subscription auth, no hard output cap, ten requests, 12 tools, one edit/check, a ten-minute deadline and two-minute provider request timeouts. Added one generic prompt instruction to trace the failing input through source and state the cause before editing. No known repair, tool, fixture or test change was supplied.

The second live run da117ff76b74443f8928767e8107a585 passed the fixed GPX/TCX/KML import check in 98.7124 seconds, with five model requests and six tool calls. The baseline passed, the seed failed and the candidate passed. All four containers were removed. This is a passing focused test and a completed Connect attempt, not independent verification, human acceptance or issue completion.

Second-run complete provider usage: 51,540 input tokens, including 12,288 cached input; 507 output tokens, zero reasoning reported; 52,047 total. Largest response 255 output tokens. Compared with the first run: 434 more total tokens (0.84%), similar runtime, and a different repair outcome. Across both attempts: 102,824 input + 836 output = 103,660 total tokens. Timing limits do not guarantee negligible token usage. One attempt per prompt is insufficient to establish why the outcome changed.

Adam narrowed current provider support to OpenAI only and explicitly deferred Claude. Keep model choice configurable within OpenAI; Claude live support is no longer a completion requirement for #104. This does not accept the stage or remove the approved-repository-instructions requirement.

Adam asked what two Needs inspection badges meant. The prepared cancelled run was a deliberate cancellation demonstration with confirmed process/container cleanup. The earlier Sol run was cancelled before inference because of a circular startup import that was subsequently fixed. Added separate report annotations; original receipt outcomes remain cancelled. Generic cancelled, failed, blocked and unfinished runs now receive specific labels.

Adam explicitly asked to proceed with #105 after walking through the shared Pi loop. This selects Verify as the next implementation stage; it does not supply unrecorded answers to the earlier review questions or mark this stage accepted.

The first Verify slice freezes a supplied patch and checks original, seeded and candidate states in a fresh source copy with the existing focused import check. Prepared examples make no model calls. Passing this focused check does not mark the candidate fully verified or the learning checkpoint reviewed. Broader required checks and live Pi retry feedback remain for later slices of #105.

Adam asked to commit the first Verify slice and continue. It was committed as f9a8d78. This authorises broader candidate checks within #105; it does not invent answers to the learning questions or approve later stages.

The second Verify slice adds fixed candidate formatting and repository make test checks while keeping source/tests read-only. Builds use a temporary bin directory. The first full attempt stopped on a tmpfs inspection mismatch, which was corrected against Podman metadata. The next ran out of temporary disk and stayed blocked. Serial, matching trimpath build settings then passed within the existing 512 MiB scratch and 1 GiB memory limits. A deliberate unformatted repair passes imports but fails formatting. No model calls or new packages were needed; the learning checkpoint still awaits discussion.

Adam asked to commit the broader checks and continue. They are committed locally as 9668edc. This selects extra independent regression cases within #105; it does not supply answers to the learning questions or approve later stages.

The third Verify slice adds trusted synthetic GPX, TCX and KML cases with different filenames and coordinates, in separate read-only verification copies. The working patch passed all eight required checks in 212.6348 seconds (e29c37c240e549048e7413e93ad5326d, nine containers removed). A deliberately filename-tailored patch passed the original test but failed all three extra cases in 150.0212 seconds (5cb7536ed8574a82a94b36d9a90a84ad, seven containers removed). The new cases also passed original source and failed the broken seed. No model ran. Permitted new files, bounded Pi feedback and the learning discussion remain pending.

Adam asked to commit the independent regression cases and continue. They are committed locally as d969607. The next slice supports explicitly permitted new source files; our learning questions remain unanswered.

The fourth Verify slice freezes permitted new source alongside existing edits. The helper-file repair passed all eight checks in 215.8162 seconds (67650cc340cd42838fe597d0e42dcb4e, nine containers removed). The deliberate addition at the protected independent-test path was refused before candidate execution (e693388d16864504b45e103eeda5fe58, three containers removed). Earlier saved Go evidence was accidentally discovered by repository Go tests; it now uses text filenames without changing its bytes, and historical receipts still match. Python policy checks and the separate Pi tests passed. No model calls, new packages or image pulls. Bounded Pi feedback and our learning review remain pending.

Adam asked to commit permitted new-file support and continue. It is committed locally as 9194aeb. The next slice connects independent check failures back to Pi with at most two repairs total and shared existing request, tool and time limits. No later stage is authorised by passing these checks.

The final Verify implementation slice connects harness_check to an independent fresh-copy verifier and permits at most two edits/checks in one Pi session, sharing 12 tool calls, the configured model-request limit and 600 seconds. Prepared SDK run 53a50109d13f4b36bb5a7bd6042b58c6 failed its first repair then passed all eight checks on the second exact patch in 331.6282 seconds; all 16 containers were removed. Prepared run 52229a7a541c488f9ce99186d305d7a0 failed both repairs and stopped at the repair limit in 197.8421 seconds; all 11 containers were removed. A deliberately unavailable immutable image stopped ddb862868dcf4b25ba0890c987f8d0b3 before Pi context, repair attempts or containers. No AI model ran. Python tests cover environment stops during verification, shared budgets, cancellation ownership, stale receipts and fabricated completion; the offline live adapter keeps one request budget across retry feedback. The learning review remains pending, and no later stage has begun.

After the harness-engineering review, Adam asked to fix clean-checkout testing and freeze checking rules, then run simplify, code-review and go-stack subagents before committing, pushing and opening a PR for Codex feedback. Python policy tests now run without Node packages; a separate pinned Pi CI job restores locked dependencies with install scripts disabled and a seven-day release cooldown. Both affected jobs fetch the pinned task history. Current frozen-evaluator-v1 sessions bind both repairs to the same tests, commands, runner source and check environment; drift stops as invalid_input. The final clean checkout passed 145 Python tests, 17 Pi tests and one separate Python-to-Pi SDK integration test. Root make test and format-check passed. Prepared run 94deb38e09e94bbf96105e1e1d7320f4 failed its first repair, then passed all eight checks on the second exact patch in 332.8033 seconds; both attempts used evaluator 76df1ef25b346e9bc4c7290318037d12c5ab5ea717442d3e250d4d2f6085c089 and all 16 containers were removed. The subagent findings were resolved. No repair-model inference was used for these demonstrations; human acceptance and the learning review remain pending.

Adam explicitly asked to pick up #106 in a new worktree. This authorises Recover implementation; it does not invent answers to the pending #105 learning questions. The first recovery path retains a one-file prepared Pi session, durable edit intents and observed hashes, reconciles disk and independent receipts before fresh context, and stops on conflict or uncertain verification. Live conversation resumption is not enabled.

The recovery code review found a cancel/publication race and malformed-journal stale success. The fixes serialize cancellation with final publication, validate journal structure, recheck final source/evidence, and keep reconstruction refusals separate from historical receipts. Per-entry Pi logs and observed partial patches are retained. Learning review remains pending.

Prepared recovery evidence: lost-reply run ace0957e6c98443188c6f84996eacdb8 resumed in 285.6675 seconds, failed its first repair then passed all eight checks on the second; all 16 containers were removed. Deliberate conflict 4e5b34fac4c1471682c62b0ee1536be9 preserved the human change and removed all three setup containers. Final checks passed 169 Python tests (24 recovery), 17 Pi tests, one SDK integration and root make test format-check. The passing real run predates the final malformed-entry validation and navigation-label fixes; the final Python suite covers those fixes. Handoff posted at https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6383961829. Work is local and uncommitted; #106 and learning review remain open.

Adam asked to commit the prepared recovery work and explain the takeaways and next step. This authorises the commit; it does not supply unrecorded learning-checkpoint answers or authorise a live model recovery run.

After committing the prepared slice as decd1d6, Adam said “great, let's go” in response to the proposed walkthrough and live recovery extension. This authorises implementing the live path and one bounded recovery demonstration using the existing Luna subscription preferences: ten model requests, twelve tools, two repairs, 600 seconds, two-minute requests and no hard output-token cap. It does not invent learning answers or stage acceptance.

Live recovery now reserves each numbered model request durably before Node can dispatch it. An uncertain request stays spent across fresh contexts. Saved model identity, twelve tools, two repairs and the original deadline are retained. The review found malformed provider-usage records could break finalization; restoration now refuses them and finalization records incomplete evidence instead of crashing. Before the bounded live demonstration, 176 Python tests (31 recovery), 21 Pi tests, one SDK integration and root make test format-check passed.

Bounded Luna subscription run 250b7c99934f407fa025ca9d485b6c9f used seven requests in its first context and the remaining three after fresh-context resume, then stopped as budget_exhausted. Both proposed edits supplied mistyped SHA-256 values and were refused. Disk had not changed; the initial description of an out-of-date hash was corrected after inspecting the receipts. Eight tool calls, zero edit intents, zero verification attempts and all three containers removed. Complete usage: 68,105 input tokens (8,064 cached), 907 output, 69,012 total, zero reported reasoning tokens. Wall time across both entries was 234.5568 seconds including the pause. The planned after-write fault was never reached. This demonstrates durable live budgets and fail-safe edit refusal, not successful live repair or applied-edit recovery. Another live run was not started after the configured limit.

Live recovery implementation and its deliberately bounded failure are documented at https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6384588837. The recommended next change is a saved-read reference while retaining Python-owned full-hash checks. New implementation remains uncommitted; no extra live run or budget increase was made.

Adam asked to commit and continue after the bounded live failure. This authorises the live-budget commit, a saved-read reference that retains Python-owned full-hash checks, and another separately bounded live recovery demonstration with the existing model and limits. The earlier run remains stopped at its original ten-request cap; learning review remains pending.

Committed the live-budget slice as 2621b28 after Adam asked to commit and continue. The next slice returns short saved-read IDs for live recovery edits; Python resolves each to its original full file hash and enforces the existing comparison. Unknown, stale and wrong-file references are refused. Completed read results survive restart; edit intents still retain normalized full-hash arguments. Before the new live demonstration, 182 Python tests (37 recovery), 22 Pi tests, one SDK integration and root make test format-check passed.

Saved-read recovery review found no actionable bugs. Live Luna run 965afc49febf4987958f18bbedeaf039 reached the deliberate after-write stop after two model requests. Fresh context reconciled the applied edit without a second write and rebuilt a planted false success summary. Its first candidate failed the independent import check. A third and final recovery entry retained the six spent requests, refused reuse of an operation ID with changed arguments, then applied a second edit on the tenth request. The task stopped budget_exhausted before checking that edit: nine tool calls, two edit intents, one failed verification, three recovery entries and seven containers removed. Complete usage: 50,203 input tokens (8,064 cached), 714 output, 50,917 total; 187.5736 seconds wall time. No successful receipt is accepted. This demonstrates actual applied-edit recovery and stale-summary resistance, not a correct model repair. Earlier failure evidence remains unchanged; learning review stays pending.

Saved-read recovery findings and four learning questions are posted at https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6384769033. Adam asked to commit and continue; the tested saved-read slice is being committed locally. Nothing is pushed, #106 stays open and the learning checkpoint remains pending.

Separate independent verification of the saved final Luna patch passed all eight required checks in run 785011ceaa084becb5253f3cdcea64de, taking 204.9462 seconds with nine containers removed and zero model calls. The original exhausted recovery receipt is byte-for-byte unchanged. Findings: https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6384913408. A passing saved patch and a completed automatic recovery session remain separate claims.

After the plain-language explanation, Adam asked to commit and continue. The existing code was already committed as e37f630; this authorises automatically checking a final saved edit when model requests run out, within the remaining tool calls and original deadline. It does not reset old sessions, raise budgets or mark the learning checkpoint accepted.

The runner now distinguishes actual model-request exhaustion from transport, output and tool failures. At the saved model limit, it can request one ordinary journaled harness_check for a pending edit and complete from exact independent receipts without a final model explanation. Handoff: https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6385077805. This is prepared boundary evidence; no new live-model run was made. Learning review remains pending.

Adam asked whether recovery was behaving as expected, which budgets applied and how to get a successful repair. The explanation distinguished safe recovery from model repair quality. The saved second Luna patch then passed separate verification; the automatic final-check extension now tests it without spending another model request. Adam asked for simpler explanations twice, so the Recover report must explain outcomes without requiring JSON or a separate chat explanation.

After asking what remained, Adam said “cool, let's go!” to the report, learning walkthrough and publication plan. This authorises the readable Recover report, commit, push and PR. It does not supply answers to the learning questions or authorise issue closure or moving to Compare. The report now includes recovery sessions and their saved journals, labels live versus prepared examples, preserves refused resumes as historical evidence and links the shared glossary.

Readable Recover report now includes recovery receipts and journals, explains each deliberate stop/reconciliation/check result, distinguishes real model work from prepared limits and retains evidence in a portable sealed snapshot. The report review found malformed top-level state, linked check output and invalid saved model settings could mislead or block reporting. Structure and link guards plus per-session error handling address those findings; the follow-up review found no actionable bugs. All 200 Python tests (34 report tests) and root make test format-check passed. Browser checks at 1280px and 390px confirmed readable results, intact section links, journal selection and explanations for every new evidence file. Findings: https://github.com/adamcbrewer/mapbox-tui/issues/106#issuecomment-6385345752. No new model call or uploaded telemetry. The first learning question is open in chat; no answer or approval has been inferred. The branch is being committed, pushed and proposed for review as authorised.

All four Recover learning questions have been discussed with Adam and his answers retained verbatim with clarifications. The discussion covered duplicate/overwritten edits after lost replies, checking actual file bytes against saved fingerprints, preserving written changes on cancellation, and investigating incomplete evidence before deciding to resume or start fresh. Adam correctly identified changed criteria and exhausted constraints as reasons to reconsider resume. The learning checkpoint is discussed and awaiting his explicit reviewed decision. At code commit 6b6ff8e, all five GitHub checks passed and Codex reported no findings; branch approval remains a separate review requirement.

All six stage HTML outputs are byte-for-byte identical under a fixed timestamp. It ran 95 focused Python and 22 Node tests. Parent verification passed 200 Python tests,22 Pi tests,1 SDK integration and root make test format-check. An additional end-to-end offline reservation/exhaustion integration test is optional, not a completion gate. The issue checklist now records twenty completed tasks; reviewed decision and report-alone walkthrough remain unchecked. Monitoring is for PR #115; no issue closure or next stage is inferred.

I asked to start #107 in a new branch/worktree after #106 closed and merged. The first step keeps every saved run, including failures, and checks that a saved pass still has matching evidence. No repair-model calls were made in that step. It doesn't establish a fair AI comparison or my approval.

I asked what #107 was actually for. I want to know whether the harness helps an AI fix bugs reliably and saves my time. I then said 'Okay, let's go.' The next prepared example compared stopping when requests run out with letting our code finish the checks. It used known working/bad fixes and no AI inference. The wider comparison remains unfinished.

I saved the plan before running eight prepared attempts. Automatic checking finished both working fixes; stopping left both unchecked. The bad fix never counted as successful. The task, exact fixes, limits and tests were the same, and I reversed the order for the second repeat. The checks took 958.8594 seconds in total; all 51 containers were removed. No repair AI or Pi session ran. This checks one part of our workflow, not AI repair skill or time saved for me. The report later gained stricter checks of failed-test evidence; the original receipts stayed intact and 228 Python tests passed. Evidence: reports/harness/compare/experiments/edc858322ce04d729a6fa0467fb8bf1b/.

I asked to commit and continue, then chose normal Pi tools inside the sandbox for the baseline. I don't want the existing four restricted tools relabelled as plain Pi. The known fixes and extra checking examples sit outside each agent project. No model call was made in this task-preparation step.

Both tasks now pass their readiness checks: the original code and known fix pass; the planted bug and ineffective edit fail on the intended assertions. I reused the unchanged development result after comparing its exact inputs, then reran the revised coordinate task. All 16 accepted saved check outputs and file fingerprints were rechecked. The final Python suite passed 238 tests, repository tests/formatting passed, and all 22 containers were removed. No repair AI or Pi session ran. I still need the normal-Pi sandbox connection before live use.

I asked for all #107 documentation, notes and summaries to use my voice and the wat skill's plain-language approach, including issue107-task-readiness.md. Future reports should explain what ran, whether an AI was involved, what worked or failed and what I can actually take from it. This is a wording request, not approval of the results or permission to close the issue.

I asked to commit and continue; the worktree was already clean at 6d1cc32. responses.question: Why isn't replaying the last tool call always safe?
responses.user_answer: The ai could find alternative solutions potentially harmful
responses.clarification: Starting over with the model can produce a different unwanted change. The immediate replay risk is that the original edit already reached disk: repeating it can duplicate work or overwrite newer content. Compare actual file bytes with the recorded before/after hashes before deciding to replay.

responses.question: When do we trust the journal, and when must we inspect disk?
responses.clarification: Events and results provide useful evidence, but may be incomplete after a crash or lost reply. Inspect the actual file bytes and compare their hash with the journalled before/after hashes: after means already applied, before permits retry, neither means conflict. Independent receipts still determine which checks completed.

responses.question: What does cancellation promise, and what changes might already exist?
responses.user_answer: Verify changes against receipts, without evidence we record the run as failed and clean up
responses.clarification: Checking evidence is necessary. Cancellation stops future work and cleans up owned processes and containers while preserving saved edits, partial patches and logs. It does not undo edits already written. Missing or uncertain evidence means cancelled/incomplete, while repair_failed means completed checks showed the candidate did not work. Unconfirmed cleanup remains explicit.

responses.question: When is starting a fresh run safer than resuming?
responses.user_answer: Criteria changed, risk of budget or constraint overflow. Incomplete is inconclusive and requires investigation rather than assuming resume is possible
responses.clarification: Changed requirements need a new task with explicit scope. Exhausted budgets remain exhausted; a new task must be a deliberate decision rather than an automatic reset. Incomplete evidence requires investigation before deciding whether safe resume or a fresh bounded task is appropriate.
